```yaml
    sets_status: Phone Verified
```

## 3. The decisions a person must always make

Two, and neither becomes a handover node. Both become the *same* booking.

| Decision | Who | What the agent does instead |
|---|---|---|
| Is this complex enough to need a CPA? | The CPA, at the consultation | Never assigns the bookkeeper. `diary.find_slots` searches CPA diaries only — there is no argument on it that could name the bookkeeper. The rate is stated; who does the work is not promised |
| What is the answer to this tax question? | A CPA, in the free half hour | Says once that it is not answered over chat, writes the question on the ticket, and books the consultation |

Making "CPA or bookkeeper" structural rather than prose is the main design decision here.
The firm's rule is that a person decides, and the reliable way to honour it is a diary the
agent cannot book the bookkeeper into, not a paragraph asking it nicely.

Tax questions get no node for the same reason dental's insurance question got none: they
arrive anywhere — mid-greeting, mid-booking — and giving every branching node a
`tax_question` way out would double the graph to model one sentence and a ticket field. It
lives in this project's `always.md`, and the CPA sees it because every path carries the
whole ticket.

Two things are *not* modelled, deliberately: nothing here is an emergency, and nothing the
CPA and the client settle in the room is relayed back through the agent.

# What you are building

A customer-service agent as **one conversation walking a graph of steps**. Not several
agents handing work to each other — one, moving through numbered nodes, carrying only what
the node it is standing in needs.

Everything a project owns lives in its own directory:

```
flow.yaml            the graph: nodes, what each is for, where each leads
always.md            the preamble every node carries
rules/<name>.md      one file per node's instructions, in prose
tools/<name>.py      tools this project wrote for itself, if any
scenarios/*.yaml     what it is tested against
business_rules.yaml  prices, hours, what we will not take on
```

## A node

```yaml
  identify:
    goal: Get their phone number, find out whether we know them, and what they came for.
    rules: [crm_lookup]                 # -> rules/crm_lookup.md
    tools: [crm.lookup_by_phone, ticket.set_fields, step.finished]
    sets_status: Phone Verified
    branch:                             # several ways out ...
      new: new_customer
      existing: warranty_check
      no_number: no_number
```

or `next: some_node` for exactly one way out, or **neither** — a node with no way out is
where the conversation ends.

Rules that the loader enforces, so a mistake fails at load rather than in front of a
customer:

- every `branch` target and every `next` must name a node that exists
- every name in `rules` must have a file in `rules/`
- every name in `tools` must be a tool that exists
- a node that is not the last one **must** have `step.finished` in its tools
- every node must be reachable from `entry`
- `goal` and `sets_status` are required; `next` and `branch` are mutually exclusive

## How a step ends

The model calls `step.finished` with an `outcome`. For a branching node the outcomes are
an **enum built from that node's own branch names**, so naming a branch that does not
exist is impossible rather than discouraged.

A last node has no `step.finished`. Its reply ends the conversation — but only once it has
called every tool it holds. A last step that says "you're all set" having booked nothing
is stopped by the engine and told what it still has to do.

## What survives a step

**Not the transcript.** When the flow moves on, the exchange is dropped and the next node
is handed a summary of the ticket: who this is, what they came about, what has been
decided. That is where the context saving comes from, and it has one hard consequence:

> **Anything a node learns and does not write down is gone.**

A node that establishes something the next one needs must put it on the ticket with
`ticket.set_fields`. This is the single commonest way a generated flow fails — a greeting
step that hears "I need to move Friday's appointment", acknowledges it warmly, and writes
nothing, so the next step asks for a phone number and nobody ever mentions Friday again.

Some facts are written by the machinery instead: a tool can declare `remembers`, and the
engine copies those fields to the ticket without the model being asked. Prefer that.

## Rules files

Prose, addressed to the step, in the company's voice. Short. What this step does, in what
order, and the one or two things that go wrong if it does otherwise.

They are assembled into the prompt when it is built, so **a long rules file is a cost paid
on every single call at that node**. Keep the whole assembled prompt under about 8,000
characters.

Write the reason, not just the rule. "Call the calendar first, on its own, and read what
comes back" is followed more reliably when it is followed by "ask for it alongside the
messages and you are writing them before you know who is going — and a name invented to
fill the gap is one the customer repeats back to somebody who has never heard it."

## Tools

A node can only name a tool that exists. Most of what a service business needs is in the
kit already — read `bat/presets/tools/service.py` before writing anything, because a tool
that is nearly the same as one you have is two tools to maintain and one of them will
drift.

When the business genuinely needs one the kit does not have, it goes in `tools/<name>.py`
in the project, and it looks like this:

```python
from bat.runtime.registry import Refused, _ticket, tool
from bat.runtime.world import AnyWorld


@tool(
    "consultant.assign",                       # the name flow.yaml uses
    "Route an enquiry to the consultant who covers that part of the world. Returns who "
    "it went to, so the reply can name them.",
    {"ticket_id": {"type": "string"},
     "destination": {"type": "string", "description": "Country or region"}},
    remembers=("consultant", "consultant_id"),  # copied to the ticket by the engine
)
def consultant_assign(world: AnyWorld, ticket_id: str, destination: str) -> dict:
    ticket = _ticket(world, ticket_id)          # raises Refused if the id is wrong
    ...
    return {"assigned": True, "consultant": "Sam", "consultant_id": "c_sam"}
```

Four things that are not optional and are each a real failure if left out:

1. **The `@tool` decorator.** A plain function in that directory is not a tool — nothing
   registers it, and `flow.yaml` naming it fails validation with "that tool does not
   exist", which reads like a typo and is not one.
2. **The description is what the model reads.** It is the only thing standing between a
   tool and being called at the wrong moment. Say what it returns, not just what it does.
3. **`remembers` names the facts that outlive the step.** The engine copies them onto the
   ticket without the model being asked. Anything the next node needs belongs here, and
   putting it here is far more reliable than telling a rules file to write it down.
4. **Raise `Refused` for something you cannot act on**, with what the caller should have
   said instead. It comes back as an answer, not a crash, and the model corrects itself.

Everything that reaches outside the process goes through a method on `world`, never
directly — `world.send_sms`, `world.notify_technician`. That is what lets the same tool run
against the simulator and against a live backend, and it is the reason these are testable
at all.

## What never goes in a rules file

- **A figure.** Prices, durations, periods come from a tool, in that conversation, or they
  are not said. A number in prose is a promise somebody else has to keep.
- **A rule the tool layer could enforce.** Anything code can refuse, code should refuse.
- **An instruction to use a tool the node does not have.** This is the most common
  configuration fault: a rules file tells a step to quote a price, `always.md` forbids
  stating a figure it has not looked up, and the node has no tool to look one up with. The
  step then refuses to answer at all — and that is your bug, not the model's.

**Tell the persona everything the customer would know.** A scenario that never gives the
customer their own phone number tests nothing but the agent's willingness to invent one —
three scenarios failed that way and the failure looked like the agent's fault.

**Write the assertions tight.** A loose assertion is worse than none: the fixing loop will
find the cheapest way to satisfy it, and that is rarely the behaviour you wanted.

# Pattern: a step that reads a choice somebody has already made

Use when the step before laid options out and this one only has to hear which.

They have been shown the options. Read what they picked and record it — that is all this
step is.

**They have usually already said it.** The answer arrives in the same breath as the
question, and the commonest failure here is asking it again: "which of the three times
works best for you" to somebody who has just written "I'll take the 11:00". Being asked
again reads as nobody listening, and it is the one thing a customer does not forgive.

Only ask if what they said genuinely does not settle it, and then ask once, plainly.

**Whatever they choose is the answer.** Do not talk them out of the expensive one, do not
push them towards it, and do not offer a view on whether their situation warrants it.

If they named a detail alongside the choice — a time, a day, a preference — write that
down too. The step that acts on it will need it and cannot see this conversation.

# Pattern: a step that lays out what is available

Say what is on offer, ask which they want, and end. **You are not waiting for the answer**
and you are not acting on it — the step after this reads what they say.

Everything you state comes from a tool, in this conversation, before you say it. Times from
the diary, figures from the rules, qualifiers included: if a fee comes back as "starting
at", that phrase goes in, because it is a floor and not a promise.

Say the part people are caught out by — the fee that is charged whether or not they go
ahead, the surcharge, the cancellation window. One sentence now prevents an argument later,
and the customer who was not told is the one who does not come back.

**If they answer before you have finished asking, that is the answer, not an instruction
you can carry out.** Do not repeat it back as settled: "11 o'clock it is" reads exactly
like a confirmation, they stop talking, and the step that would have made it true never
runs. Take it down and end the step. The next one confirms it, because the next one can.

# Pattern: the step that actually commits something

**Do the committing call first, on its own, and read what comes back.** It returns who is
assigned and the time as it should be said. Ask for it alongside the messages and you are
writing them before you know either — and a name invented to fill the gap is one the
customer repeats back to somebody who has never heard it.

Then, with that answer in front of you, the rest together: tell the person doing the work,
tell the customer, and arrange the follow-up.

**The person doing the work before the customer.** A confirmation for a visit nobody has
been told about is worse than no confirmation: the customer stops worrying about something
nobody is coming to.

**One message to the customer, right the first time.** A correction leaves them with two
versions of when somebody is coming and no way to tell which is current.

Say the cancellation terms here if there are any. This is the moment they are agreeing to
them, and the only moment saying so is not an ambush.

Then tell them what happens next and that they do not need to wait here.

# Pattern: a step that hands work to a person

Use for any ending where a human takes over: a claim to judge, a quote to price, somebody
who needs help now, a booking to rearrange.

Once this is with a person, you are done managing it.

Raise it with everything on the ticket, and a reason that says **which kind** of handover
this is. "Escalated" alone tells the person nothing about what they are opening.

Then arrange a follow-up, 24 hours out. **Handing work to a person is not the work being
done**, and nothing else in the system notices if they never get to it. Somebody asks them
tomorrow, and every day after that until they answer.

Then tell the customer, on that turn — not the next one. Say it as what it is: their job
is with a named person and that person will come back to them.

**Do not stay to be sympathetic.** Somebody upset will keep asking, and every answer is
another round in a step that has already done everything it can. One step spent four turns
being kind to an angry customer while the person who could actually settle it had not been
told yet.

**End the conversation. Do not close the ticket.** Work nobody has done yet is not
finished work, and a closed ticket is one nobody checks back on.

# Pattern: a step that turns work away

Say what cannot be done, say why in one sentence, and close.

Use the owner's own wording, stored in `business_rules.yaml` and read from a tool. This is
the sentence most likely to be repeated to somebody else, quoted back, or screenshotted,
and a paraphrase of a referral number is a wrong number.

**Do not hint that an exception exists.** No "normally", no "in most cases", no suggestion
that describing it differently or asking somebody senior might work. A clean no is more use
to them than a soft one — a soft no sends people away to try again in a fortnight.

If the refusal has somewhere else to send them, send them there in the same breath, with
the name and the number. A decline that ends in a door is different from one that ends in a
direction, and only one of them is remembered kindly.

Where the business would still take other work from this person, say so plainly. "We don't
do that, but we'd be glad to see you for X" keeps a customer that a flat refusal loses.

```
always.md            the preamble every node carries
```

```yaml

    goal: Get their phone number, find out whether we know them, and what they came for.
    rules: [crm_lookup]                 # -> rules/crm_lookup.md
    tools: [crm.lookup_by_phone, ticket.set_fields, step.finished]
```

Rules that the loader enforces, so a mistake fails at load rather than in front of a
customer:

- every `branch` target and every `next` must name a node that exists
- every name in `rules` must have a file in `rules/`
- every name in `tools` must be a tool that exists

an **enum built from that node's own branch names**, so naming a branch that does not
exist is impossible rather than discouraged.

called every tool it holds. A last step that says "you're all set" having booked nothing
is stopped by the engine and told what it still has to do.

step that hears "I need to move Friday's appointment", acknowledges it warmly, and writes
nothing, so the next step asks for a phone number and nobody ever mentions Friday again.

Some facts are written by the machinery instead: a tool can declare `remembers`, and the
engine copies those fields to the ticket without the model being asked. Prefer that.

   putting it here is far more reliable than telling a rules file to write it down.
4. **Raise `Refused` for something you cannot act on**, with what the caller should have
   said instead. It comes back as an answer, not a crash, and the model corrects itself.

Everything that reaches outside the process goes through a method on `world`, never
directly — `world.send_sms`, `world.notify_technician`. That is what lets the same tool run
against the simulator and against a live backend, and it is the reason these are testable
at all.

## 3. The decisions a person must always make

Two, and neither becomes a handover node. Both become the *same* booking.

| Decision | Who | What the agent does instead |
|---|---|---|
| Is this complex enough to need a CPA? | The CPA, at the consultation | Never assigns the bookkeeper. `diary.find_slots` searches CPA diaries only — there is no argument on it that could name the bookkeeper. The rate is stated; who does the work is not promised |
| What is the answer to this tax question? | A CPA, in the free half hour | Says once that it is not answered over chat, writes the question on the ticket, and books the consultation |

Making "CPA or bookkeeper" structural rather than prose is the main design decision here.
The firm's rule is that a person decides, and the reliable way to honour it is a diary the
agent cannot book the bookkeeper into, not a paragraph asking it nicely.

Tax questions get no node for the same reason dental's insurance question got none: they
arrive anywhere — mid-greeting, mid-booking — and giving every branching node a
`tax_question` way out would double the graph to model one sentence and a ticket field. It
lives in this project's `always.md`, and the CPA sees it because every path carries the
whole ticket.

Two things are *not* modelled, deliberately: nothing here is an emergency, and nothing the
CPA and the client settle in the room is relayed back through the agent.

**From the kit, unchanged (7):** `crm.lookup_by_phone` · `ticket.set_fields` · `clock.now` ·

| Tool | Why it is not a preset |
|---|---|
| `client.create` | `crm.create_customer` demands a service address and has nowhere for a preferred language or personal-vs-corporate. Nobody goes out, so there is no address to ask for |
| `client.work_in_progress` | `crm.get_warranty_candidates` is worded around an address and a warranty claim. This is "what do we have in hand and what state is it in" |
| `rules.get_fees` | One call: both personal tiers, the corporate starting-at **and** the sentence that a CPA quotes it after seeing the books, the bookkeeping rate, the free half hour, and the no-surcharge line. | `rules.deadline_pressure` | Days between now and 30 April, and a band. The model never does arithmetic on a date, and "you should come in sooner" is not a feeling |

code is followed every time:

- **Never assign the bookkeeper** — `diary.find_slots` cannot return their slot.
- **Saturdays only in tax season** — `diary.find_slots` cannot return 12 July at 11:00.
- **Closed Sundays, evenings, BC statutory holidays** — same tool.
- **In person or on video is recorded** — `diary.book` refuses without a mode, so a booking
  where nobody said which never reaches the diary, and the confirmation text can carry the
  address or the video link rather than a guess.
- **Which personal tier** — `rules.price_personal_return` decides.
- **Never quote a corporate year-end** — `rules.get_fees` returns a sentence to say instead
  of a total, alongside the starting-at figure and its qualifier.
- **Deadline urgency** — `rules.deadline_pressure` returns the band and the days.
- **One recipient for handovers** — no id argument anywhere.

# Model provider configuration (OpenAI-compatible API).
#
# Two providers are defined below and one is active. **Switching is the `active:` line
# and nothing else** — the roles get their model id from the active provider, so a
# switch does not mean editing seven role blocks and missing one.
#
# The API key never lives here. It is read from .env under the variable named by
# api_key_env, and <NAME>_BASE_URL overrides base_url for that provider.
#
# If a model id returns 404, run `python3 scripts/check_llm.py` to list the real ids.

# Bailian shook the new paths out and reached 82% (23/28), which was the agreed line for
# coming back here. Everything it caught was a rules file or a scenario of ours, not the
# endpoint — which is the point of doing it on the cheaper one first.
# Bailian for building and iterating, DeepSeek's own endpoint for the verdict.
#
# They are the same model family and measurably not the same thing: on a 28-run suite,
# 82% here against 84-90% there, and 60% cache hits against 84%. That gap is the reason
# to develop on this one — a failure that shows up on the cheaper endpoint is almost
# always a rules file or a scenario of ours, and those are the failures worth finding.
# Switch to `deepseek` before calling a project finished.
active: bailian-deepseek

providers:
  # Not active. A full 24-scenario baseline came back 4/24 against DeepSeek's 21/24, with
  # every failure the agent's and all of one shape: tools it was told to call and did not,
  # handoffs not made, states walked wrong. Its cache also only reached 14.2% against
  # DeepSeek's 94%, so the input cost was roughly sixteen times higher in practice.
  # Kept for a retry with explicit cache_control and thinking on for the agent.
  qwen:
    base_url: "https://llm-lhu6gyj1f60ryppl.cn-beijing.maas.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1"
    api_key_env: "QWEN_API_KEY"
    model: "qwen3.7-flash"
    timeout_seconds: 120
    max_retries: 3
    # Vendor switches with no field in the OpenAI schema. Qwen reasons by default and
    # bills the thinking as output tokens: on a trivial question that was 194 output
    # tokens instead of 6, for an identical answer. Off globally; a role can override.
    extra_body:
      enable_thinking: false
    # Its json_object mode refuses unless the word "json" appears somewhere in the
    # messages. Every prompt that asks for JSON here already says so, but a new one
    # must too, or the call comes back 400.

  # DeepSeek's model served from Bailian, so the key and the billing sit in one place.
  # No provider-level extra_body: this one reasons natively and both directions of
  # enable_thinking work, so the roles decide. Nothing is turned off here that has not
  # been measured — turning it off untested cost a whole 24-scenario baseline today.
  bailian-deepseek:
    base_url: "https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1"
    api_key_env: "QWEN_API_KEY"
    model: "deepseek-v4-flash-0731"
    timeout_seconds: 120
    max_retries: 3

  # Active. Same model family as the Bailian entry below it, and measurably not the same
  # thing: on the flow suite, twenty-three of twenty-four against nineteen, with no model
  # faults at all against four. Cache hits 81% against 62%, which more than halves the
  # input billed at full price — a single probe showed it caching 1,536 of 1,555 tokens
  # where Bailian cached 1,024 of 1,476, so the prefix is cut more finely.
  #
  # Worth writing down because it was nearly missed: the endpoint had been treated as an
  # implementation detail of the model, and the gap between them was read as the ceiling
  # of what this model could do.
  deepseek:
    base_url: "https://api.deepseek.com/v1"
    api_key_env: "DEEPSEEK_API_KEY"
    model: "deepseek-v4-flash"
    timeout_seconds: 120
    max_retries: 3
    # Also a reasoning model, but with no switch to turn the thinking off — budget
    # max_tokens for it. Cache hit rates of 93-94% were normal on this workload.

# Per-role settings. The model comes from the active provider; add `model: "..."` to a
# role only when that role should differ from the rest.
roles:
  builder:                                # The generator's own tool loop (bat/builder/agent.py)
    # Thinking ON. Deciding which file to write next from what the last one contained is
    # reasoning, and this role writes twenty-odd files off one brief.
    extra_body: { enable_thinking: true }
    temperature: 0.2                      # Writing config and prose to a spec, not chatting
    max_tokens: 8000                      # A rules file plus a flow.yaml in one answer
  agent:                                  # Business agents (intake / small_job / ...)
    # Thinking ON. It was off on the grounds that this is a conversational role, and the
    # full baseline came back 4/24 against DeepSeek's 21/24 — every failure the agent's,
    # and all of one shape: tools it was told to call and did not, handoffs not made,
    # states walked wrong. Deciding which tool to call next from what the last one
    # returned is reasoning, whatever the output looks like to a customer.
    extra_body: { enable_thinking: true }
    temperature: 0.3
    max_tokens: 2000
  customer:                               # Simulated customer
    temperature: 0.9                      # High temperature -> varied wording, real pressure-testing
    max_tokens: 500
  technician:                             # Simulated technician (on-site staff)
    temperature: 0.7
    max_tokens: 400
  supervisor:                             # Simulated supervisor
    temperature: 0.5
    max_tokens: 500
  judge:                                  # LLM judge (rule-compliance verdicts)
    extra_body: { enable_thinking: true }
    temperature: 0.0                      # Verdicts must be stable
    max_tokens: 1500

  # Thinking stays on for the roles whose whole job is cross-referencing. Measured on the
  # 1300-line corpus with it off: output fell from 44,574 tokens to 903, and three of the
  # four findings were wrong — one of them contradicted the evidence it had just quoted.
  # The saving was the model not doing the work. These roles run rarely; the volume is in
  # the conversational roles above, and those keep thinking off.
  auditor:                                # Static consistency scan over all prompts
    extra_body: { enable_thinking: true }
    temperature: 0.0                      # Same corpus must give the same findings
    # Reads the whole prompt corpus with thinking on, and reasoning bills against this.
    # Measured across five runs on a corpus that grew 1.7%: output went 11,331 -> 14,028
    # -> 13,834 -> 19,696 -> past 48,000. The corpus is not what moves this; how long it
    # decides to think is, and the spread is wide enough that any budget near the average
    # is a cliff. An exhausted budget returns an empty reply after several minutes and
    # reports nothing; unused budget costs nothing at all. So it is set well clear.
    max_tokens: 120000
    # Longer than the provider default of 120s. This call reads 1400 lines and reasons over
    # all of it; measured runs take two to four minutes, and it has died at the two-minute
    # mark. Overrides `providers.*.timeout_seconds` for this role only — the conversational
    # roles keep the short one, where a slow call really is a broken call.
    timeout_seconds: 600
    # No retry. This times out for one reason — it thought for the whole window — and that
    # reason does not go away on a second attempt. Three retries turned a ten-minute
    # failure into a forty-minute one with the same result.
    max_retries: 0

  doctor:                                 # Only used when doctor_backend.kind = "openai"
    extra_body: { enable_thinking: true }
    temperature: 0.4
    max_tokens: 8000

# Which engine rewrites agent prompts when a scenario fails.
#
#   claude_cli - shell out to the Claude Code CLI with permission checks bypassed, so a
#                strong model can read the repo and edit prompt files directly. Guards are
#                enforced afterwards: every protected file is hashed before and after, and
#                the whole attempt is discarded if anything outside agents/ was touched.
#   openai     - one-shot JSON patch from the `doctor` role above (no repo access).
#
# `command` is optional and only needed when the binary is somewhere unusual — say
# "/root/.local/bin/claude". Without it doctor tries PATH and then the places the
# installer normally uses, which covers the common case: the CLI installed under
# ~/.local/bin while nothing has put that directory on any PATH.
doctor_backend:
  kind: "claude_cli"
  model: "claude-opus-5"
  timeout_seconds: 900
  extra_args: []

# Per-scenario ceilings, so a stuck agent cannot burn tokens indefinitely
limits:
  # A full journey runs intake -> a service agent -> waiting on the technician -> closing,
  # so it needs considerably more room than a single-agent test.
  max_conversation_turns: 45              # Customer <-> agent exchanges
  max_tool_calls_per_turn: 15             # Consecutive tool calls within one turn
  max_handoffs: 5                         # Agent handoffs within one scenario
  # Turns the agent gets after the customer leaves, to finish the ticket.
  max_wrapup_turns: 8
  # A scheduled follow-up wakes the agent back up, as a real scheduler would.
  max_followup_firings: 3
  # Scenarios are independent, so they parallelise cleanly. Raise this to cut wall
  # clock time; lower it if the provider rate-limits you.
  parallel_scenarios: 5
